notes.front: What is a magneto?
notes.back: A special type of engine-driven alternating current generator that uses a permanent magnet as its source of energy.
notes.explanation: It makes current from three things together: a permanent magnet, a coil of wire and relative movement between them.
notes.example: Like a bicycle dynamo, which makes current from a spinning magnet, but timed to the engine to fire spark plugs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magneto-Ignition System Operating Principles”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: The magneto, a special type of engine-driven alternating current (AC) generator, uses a permanent magnet as a source of energy. By the use of a permanent magnet (basic magnetic field), coil of wire (concentrated lengths of conductor), and relative movement of the magnetic field, current is generated in the wire.

notes.front: What does a spark plug do in an ignition system?
notes.back: It conducts a short high-voltage impulse through the combustion chamber wall and provides an air gap for the spark.
notes.explanation: The spark across that gap is what ignites the air-fuel charge inside the cylinder.
notes.example: Like the igniter on a gas hob, but screwed into the cylinder head and fired by the engine’s ignition system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: The function of the spark plug in an ignition system is to conduct a short impulse of high-voltage current through the wall of the combustion chamber. Inside the combustion chamber, it provides an air gap across which the impulse can produce an electric spark to ignite the air-fuel charge.

notes.front: What is a high-tension magneto system?
notes.back: A magneto system that contains the high voltage all the way from the magneto until it passes through the spark plug.
notes.explanation: That was its early weakness: the lead materials of the time could not withstand the voltage and leaked to ground.
notes.example: Like a hose kept at full pressure from the tap right to the nozzle, rather than boosted only at the nozzle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: the high-tension system that was containing the high-voltage until it passed through the spark plug. The materials that were used for ignition leads could not withstand the high-voltage and were prone to leak to ground before the spark would get to the cylinder.

notes.front: What makes up the magnetic circuit of a magneto?
notes.back: A permanent multi-pole rotating magnet, a soft iron core and pole shoes.
notes.explanation: The magnet is geared to the engine and turns between the pole shoes to supply the flux needed to produce a voltage.
notes.example: Like a bar magnet spinning between the jaws of a soft iron horseshoe, but with several poles.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magnetic Circuit”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: The magnetic circuit consists of a permanent multi-pole rotating magnet, a soft iron core, and pole shoes. [Figure 4-3] The magnet is geared to the aircraft engine and rotates in the gap between two pole shoes to furnish the magnetic lines of force (flux) necessary to produce an electrical voltage.

notes.front: What three parts make up a magneto’s primary electrical circuit?
notes.back: Breaker contact points, a condenser and an insulated coil.
notes.explanation: Its coil is only a few turns of heavy copper wire, grounded to the coil core at one end and wired to the points at the other.
notes.example: Like a doorbell circuit with a push switch, but the switch is a pair of points opened by a cam.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The primary electrical circuit consists of a set of breaker contact points, a condenser, and an insulated coil. [Figure 4-5] The coil is made up of a few turns of heavy copper wire, one end is grounded to the coil core and the other end to the ungrounded side of the breaker points.

notes.front: Where is the condenser wired in a magneto’s primary circuit?
notes.back: In parallel with the breaker points.
notes.explanation: There it stops arcing at the points when they open and speeds the collapse of the magnetic field around the primary coil.
notes.example: Like a small reservoir beside a tap that soaks up the surge when the tap snaps shut.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The third unit in the circuit, the condenser (capacitor), is wired in parallel with the breaker points. The condenser prevents arcing at the points when the circuit is opened and hastens the collapse of the magnetic field about the primary coil.

notes.front: What is the E-gap position of a magneto?
notes.back: The point a few degrees beyond neutral that the rotating magnet reaches before the points open; the E stands for efficiency.
notes.explanation: Current in the primary circuit holds the core flux high in one direction until the magnet has turned this far.
notes.example: Like drawing a catapult back past its resting point before letting go, but measured in degrees of magnet rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: the current flowing in the primary circuit holds the flux in the core at a high value in one direction until the rotating magnet has time to rotate through the neutral position to a point a few degrees beyond neutral. This position is called the E-gap position (E stands for efficiency).

notes.front: What does a magneto’s secondary circuit contain?
notes.back: The secondary coil windings and the parts that carry their output: the distributor, the ignition lead and the spark plug.
notes.explanation: Its coil is a winding of about 13,000 turns of fine insulated wire, far more than the primary’s few turns.
notes.example: Like the high-pressure outlet pipework of a pump, but carrying voltage to the spark plugs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The secondary circuit contains the secondary windings of the coil, distributor rotor, distributor cap, ignition lead, and spark plug. The secondary coil is made up of a winding containing approximately 13,000 turns of fine, insulated wire;

notes.front: What are the two parts of a magneto’s distributor?
notes.back: A revolving distributor rotor and a stationary distributor block.
notes.explanation: The high voltage from the secondary coil is sent to the distributor, whose rotor turns inside the fixed block.
notes.example: Like a rotating sorter at a post office, handing each letter to the right slot in turn, but with sparks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The high-voltage induced in the secondary coil is directed to the distributor, which consists of two parts: revolving and stationary. The revolving part is called a distributor rotor and the stationary part is called a distributor block.

notes.front: What does an ignition harness contain?
notes.back: An insulated wire for each cylinder the magneto serves, running from the distributor block to the proper spark plug.
notes.explanation: Each lead is the path that directs the magneto’s electrical energy to its spark plug.
notes.example: Like the cables from a hi-fi amplifier to each speaker, but shielded and carrying spark voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness”, p. 4-7
notes.evidence: The ignition lead directs the electrical energy from the magneto to the spark plug. The ignition harness contains an insulated wire for each cylinder that the magneto serves in the engine. [Figure 4-11] One end of each wire is connected to the magneto distributor block and the other end is connected to the proper spark plug.

notes.front: What is a P-lead?
notes.back: The primary lead: the wire that connects a magneto’s primary winding to the ignition switch.
notes.explanation: Grounding this wire is what turns the magneto off.
notes.example: Like a kill cord on a jet ski, except the magneto stops only while this wire is grounded.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Glossary: P-lead”, p. G-20
notes.evidence: P-lead. Primary lead. The wire that connects the primary winding of a magneto to the ignition switch. The magneto is turned off by grounding its P-lead.

notes.front: How is a flange-mounted magneto attached to the engine?
notes.back: By a flange around the driven end of the magneto’s rotating shaft.
notes.explanation: Elongated slots in the flange allow limited adjustment to help time the magneto to the engine.
notes.example: Like a light fitting held by screws in slotted holes, which can be turned a little before the screws are tightened.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magneto Mounting Systems”, p. 4-10
notes.evidence: Flange-mounted magnetos are attached to the engine by a flange around the driven end of the rotating shaft of the magneto. [Figure 4-19] Elongated slots in the mounting flange permit adjustment through a limited range to aid in timing the magneto to the engine.

notes.front: In a FADEC system for a reciprocating engine, what is the electronic control unit (ECU)?
notes.back: The heart of the system: a unit giving both ignition and fuel injection control, with two microprocessors controlling two cylinders.
notes.explanation: Each of its computers controls its own cylinder and can give redundant control for the other computer’s cylinder.
notes.example: Like the engine computer in a modern car, but with one unit for each pair of cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-15
notes.evidence: The ECU is at the heart of the system, providing both ignition and fuel injection control to operate the engine with the maximum efficiency realizable. Each ECU contains two microprocessors, referred to as a computer, that control two cylinders. Each computer controls its own assigned cylinder and is capable of providing redundant control for the other computer’s cylinder.

notes.front: What is the low-voltage harness of a FADEC system?
notes.back: A signal transfer bus linking the ECUs with aircraft power, the ignition switch and the engine’s sensors.
notes.explanation: It carries the sensor inputs to the ECUs through a 50-pin connector.
notes.example: Like the data cabling in an office linking every desk to the server, but on an engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Low-Voltage Harness”, p. 4-15
notes.evidence: units (ECUs) with aircraft power sources, the ignition switch, speed sensor assembly (SSA), temperature and pressure sensors. The fuel injector coils and all sensors, except the SSA and fuel pressure and manifold pressure sensors, are hardwired to the low-voltage harness. This harness transmits sensor inputs to the ECUs through a 50-pin connector.

notes.front: What does the PowerLink FADEC system do if primary aircraft-supplied power is lost?
notes.back: Its engine controls keep operating on a secondary power source.
notes.explanation: The system is designed to give control in fault conditions as well as normal ones and to prevent adverse changes in power.
notes.example: Like a computer on an uninterruptible power supply, but it runs a piston engine’s ignition and fuel injection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-14
notes.evidence: PowerLink provides control in both specified operating conditions and fault conditions. The system is designed to prevent adverse changes in power or thrust. In the event of loss of primary aircraft-supplied power, the engine controls continue to operate using a secondary power source (SPS).

notes.front: What is a booster coil?
notes.back: An older auxiliary starting unit, separate from the magneto, that generates its own series of sparks for starting.
notes.explanation: It was used mainly with older radial engine ignition systems and is built from two coils, contact points and a condenser.
notes.example: Like a jump-starter pack, but supplying sparks rather than cranking power.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Booster Coil”, p. 4-18
notes.evidence: Used mainly with older radial engine ignition systems, the booster coil assembly consists of two coils wound on a soft iron core, a set of contact points, and a condenser. [Figure 4-31] The booster coil is separate from the magneto and can generate a series of sparks on its own.

notes.front: What is an impulse coupling?
notes.back: A cam, flyweight and spring device that gives one magneto, generally the left, a brief acceleration to produce an intense starting spark.
notes.explanation: It sits between the engine drive and the magneto, so the spring can hold the magneto back and then release it.
notes.example: Like winding a clockwork toy and letting it snap free, but the snap spins the magneto.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Impulse Coupling”, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: engine, generally the left, a brief acceleration, that produces an intense spark for starting. This device consists of a cam and flyweight assembly, spring, and a body assembly.

notes.front: What is the shower of sparks system?
notes.back: A starting system whose starting vibrator gives several sparks at the spark plug electrodes during starting.
notes.explanation: It was developed to give more spark power while starting; its vibrator unit is essentially a vibrator, a condenser and a relay.
notes.example: Like a doorbell buzzer, but its buzzing chops battery current into the magneto.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Retard Breaker Vibrator”, p. 4-21
notes.evidence: To provide for more spark power during the starting cycle, the shower of sparks system was developed, which provides several sparks at the spark plug electrodes during starting. The starting vibrator, or shower of sparks, consists essentially of an electrically operated vibrator, a condenser, and a relay.

notes.front: What does a retard breaker vibrator system add to the magneto to get retarded starting sparks?
notes.back: An additional breaker, the retard points, used together with a starting vibrator.
notes.explanation: Designed for four- and six-cylinder systems, it removes the need for an impulse coupling in light aircraft.
notes.example: Like a second, later light switch that takes over only while starting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Retard Breaker Vibrator”, p. 4-22
notes.evidence: Designed for four- and six-cylinder ignition systems, the retard breaker magneto eliminates the need for the impulse coupling in light aircraft. This system uses an additional breaker to obtain retarded sparks for starting.

notes.front: What is the heat range of a spark plug?
notes.back: A measure of its ability to transfer the heat of combustion to the cylinder head.
notes.explanation: The plug must run hot enough to burn off carbon deposits that cause fouling, yet cool enough to prevent pre-ignition.
notes.example: Like choosing between a thin and a thick pan handle, but here it is how fast heat leaves the plug’s tip.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: The heat range of a spark plug is a measure of its ability to transfer the heat of combustion to the cylinder head. The plug must operate hot enough to burn off carbon deposits, which can cause fouling, a condition where the plug no longer produces a spark across the electrodes, yet remain cool enough to prevent a pre-ignition condition.

notes.front: What is spark plug reach?
notes.back: The length of the threaded portion that goes into the cylinder’s spark plug bushing.
notes.explanation: The right reach puts the electrode end in the best position inside the cylinder to achieve ignition.
notes.example: Like the length of a screw, which has to suit the thickness of what it goes into.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: A spark plug with the proper reach ensures that the electrode end inside the cylinder is in the best position to achieve ignition. The spark plug reach is the length of the threaded portion that is inserted in the spark plug bushing of the cylinder.

notes.front: Where are built-in timing marks usually found on a reciprocating engine?
notes.back: On the starter gear hub if one is fitted; otherwise normally on the propeller flange edge.
notes.explanation: Most reciprocating engines have such marks, but where they sit varies by manufacturer.
notes.example: Like the alignment arrows on a camera lens, but marking degrees of crankshaft rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Built-In Engine Timing Reference Marks”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: The timing reference marks vary by manufacturer. [Figure 4-43] When the starter gear hub is installed correctly, the timing marks are marked on it that line up with the mark on the starter. On an engine that has no starter gear hub, the timing mark is normally on the propeller flange edge.

notes.front: What is a timing disc?
notes.back: A timing plate temporarily fitted to the crankshaft flange, with a scale in crankshaft degrees and a pointer.
notes.explanation: Its markings vary with the specifications of the engine it is used on.
notes.example: Like a protractor clamped to a wheel, but read against crankshaft rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing Discs”, p. 4-27
notes.evidence: Most timing disc devices are mounted to the crankshaft flange and use a timing plate. [Figure 4-46] The markings vary according to the specifications of the engine. This plate is temporarily installed on the crankshaft flange with a scale numbered in crankshaft degrees and the pointer attached to the timing disc.

notes.front: To which piston position is every piston position indicator reading referenced?
notes.back: Top dead centre, whether the reading is for ignition, valve or injection pump timing.
notes.explanation: Top dead centre must not be confused with top centre, a different piston position.
notes.example: Like a finish-line camera that fixes one exact moment, but fixing where the piston is.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Piston Position Indicators”, p. 4-27
notes.evidence: Any given piston position, whether it is to be used for ignition, valve, or injection pump timing, is referenced to a piston position called top dead center. This piston position is not to be confused with a piston position called top center.

notes.front: What is a timing light used for?
notes.back: Finding the exact instant the magneto’s breaker points open.
notes.explanation: Both common types have two lights and three external wire connections, so two sets of points can be watched.
notes.example: Like a continuity tester’s bulb, but showing the moment the points separate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing Lights”, p. 4-28
notes.evidence: Timing lights are used to help determine the exact instant that the magneto points open. There are two general types of timing lights in common use. Both have two lights and three external wire connections.

notes.front: What is carbon fouling from fuel associated with?
notes.back: Mixtures too rich to burn, or so lean that they cause intermittent firing.
notes.explanation: Each time a plug fails to fire, raw fuel and oil collect on its electrodes and nose insulator.
notes.example: Like the soot on a smoky candle wick, but on the plug’s firing end.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Carbon Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-33
notes.evidence: Carbon fouling from fuel is associated with mixtures that are too rich to burn or mixtures that are so lean they cause intermittent firing. [Figure 4-55] Each time a spark plug does not fire, raw fuel and oil collect on the nonfiring electrodes and nose insulator.

notes.front: How does oil fouling stop a spark plug working?
notes.back: Oil drawn into the cylinder combines with soot at low engine speed to form a solid that can short out the plug.
notes.explanation: Oil gets in past the piston rings, valve guides and impeller shaft seal rings even when the idle mixture is correct.
notes.example: Like a wet cable shorting out a socket, but with oily soot bridging the electrodes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-34
notes.evidence: Even though the idling air-fuel mixture is correct, there is a tendency for oil to be drawn into the cylinder past the piston rings, valve guides, and impeller shaft oil seal rings. At low engine speeds, the oil combines with the soot in the cylinder to form a solid that is capable of shorting out the spark plug.

notes.front: What is lead fouling of a spark plug?
notes.back: Deposits of lead oxide, formed when leaded fuel burns, that stop the plug working normally.
notes.explanation: Lead is added to aviation fuel for its anti-knock qualities, but it forms lead oxide during combustion.
notes.example: Like limescale building up inside a kettle, but formed from the fuel’s lead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Lead Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-34
notes.evidence: Lead fouling of aviation spark plugs is a condition likely to occur in any engine using leaded fuels. Lead is added to aviation fuel to improve its anti-knock qualities. The lead, however, has the undesirable effect of forming lead oxide during combustion.

notes.front: What causes graphite fouling of spark plugs?
notes.back: Careless, excessive antiseize thread lubricant flowing over the electrodes and shorting them.
notes.explanation: Graphite is a good electrical conductor, so it gives the spark an easy path.
notes.example: Like pencil lead drawn across a circuit board, but smeared on by greasy fingers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Graphite Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: As a result of careless and excessive application of thread lubricant, called antiseize compound, to the spark plug, the lubricant flows over the electrodes and causes shorting. Shorting occurs because graphite is a good electrical conductor.

notes.front: What is spark plug gap erosion?
notes.back: Wear of the electrodes as each spark carries off some electrode metal, widening the air gap.
notes.explanation: Part of the metal lands on the other electrode and the rest is blown off into the combustion chamber.
notes.example: Like a pencil point wearing blunt, but a speck of metal goes with every spark.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gap Erosion of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: Erosion of the electrodes takes place in all aircraft spark plugs as the spark jumps the air gap between the electrodes. [Figure 4-57] The spark carries with it a portion of the electrode, part of which is deposited on the other electrode. The remainder is blown off in the combustion chamber.

notes.front: What is a capacitor discharge ignition system, as fitted to the typical turbine engine?
notes.back: Two identical, independent ignition units working from a common low-voltage direct current power source.
notes.explanation: The power can come from the aircraft battery, 115 volts alternating current or the engine’s permanent magnet generator.
notes.example: Like a camera flash that charges a capacitor and then dumps it, but firing a turbine’s igniter.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-43
notes.evidence: The typical turbine engine is equipped with a capacitor-type, or capacitor discharge, ignition system consisting of two identical independent ignition units operating from a common low-voltage (DC) electrical power source: the aircraft battery, 115AC, or its permanent magnet generator.

notes.front: In a capacitor discharge exciter unit, where is the ignition energy stored?
notes.back: In capacitors: each discharge circuit has two storage capacitors, both inside the exciter unit.
notes.explanation: Like other turbine ignition, it is needed only for starting, because once combustion begins the flame is continuous.
notes.example: Like the charging box of a camera flash, but sealed, doubled and bolted to an engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Capacitor Discharge Exciter Unit”, p. 4-44
notes.evidence: Like other turbine ignition systems, it is required only for starting the engine; once combustion has begun, the flame is continuous. [Figure 4-74] The energy is stored in capacitors. Each discharge circuit incorporates two storage capacitors; both are located in the exciter unit.

notes.front: What sets a turbine igniter plug apart from a reciprocating engine’s spark plug?
notes.back: Its electrode must withstand current of much higher energy than a conventional spark plug electrode.
notes.explanation: That current can quickly erode the electrode, but the short periods of operation keep this in check.
notes.example: Like a spark plug, but built for rare, very powerful sparks instead of constant ones.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Igniter Plugs”, p. 4-45
notes.evidence: Its electrode must be capable of withstanding a current of much higher energy than the electrode of a conventional spark plug. This high energy current can quickly cause electrode erosion, but the short periods of operation minimize this aspect of igniter maintenance.

notes.front: What is an engine starter?
notes.back: An electromechanical mechanism that develops large amounts of mechanical energy to turn an engine for starting.
notes.explanation: Most aircraft engines, reciprocating or turbine, need this help during the starting process.
notes.example: Like the starter motor in a car, though some aircraft starters run on air or a flywheel instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Starting Systems: Introduction”, p. 5-1
notes.evidence: Most aircraft engines, reciprocating or turbine, require help during the starting process. Hence, this device is termed the starter. A starter is an electromechanical mechanism capable of developing large amounts of mechanical energy that can be applied to an engine, causing it to rotate.

notes.front: What does an inertia starter rely on to crank the engine?
notes.back: Kinetic energy stored in a rapidly rotating flywheel.
notes.explanation: Hand, electric and combined hand-and-electric inertia starters all work this way.
notes.example: Like a spinning top wound up and then released, but coupled to the crankshaft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inertia Starters”, p. 5-1
notes.evidence: There are three general types of inertia starters: hand, electric, and combination hand and electric. The operation of all types of inertia starters depends on the kinetic energy stored in a rapidly rotating flywheel for cranking ability.

notes.front: What is a direct cranking electric starter?
notes.back: An electric motor, reduction gears and an automatic engaging mechanism that crank the engine instantly and continually when energised.
notes.explanation: It is the most widely used starting system on all types of reciprocating engines.
notes.example: Like a car’s starter motor, which cranks for as long as the key is held.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starter”, p. 5-2
notes.evidence: The most widely used starting system on all types of reciprocating engines utilizes the direct cranking electric starter. This type of starter provides instant and continual cranking when energized. The direct cranking electric starter consists basically of an electric motor, reduction gears, and an automatic engaging and disengaging mechanism that is operated through an adjustable torque overload release clutch.

notes.front: In an automatic small-aircraft starting system, what does the starter solenoid do?
notes.back: When a push button or the ignition key activates it, its contacts close and energise the starter motor.
notes.explanation: The motor’s first rotation then engages the starter through an overrunning clutch in the starter adapter.
notes.example: Like a relay that lets a small switch control a large current, but sized for a starter motor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starting System for Small Aircraft”, p. 5-6
notes.evidence: A starter solenoid is activated by either a push button or turning the ignition key on the instrument panel. When the solenoid is activated, its contacts close, and electrical energy energizes the starter motor. Initial rotation of the starter motor engages the starter through an overrunning clutch in the starter adapter, which incorporates worm reduction gears.

notes.front: What must a turbine engine starter do?
notes.back: Accelerate the compressor until there is enough air for combustion, then keep helping after light-off until self-sustaining speed.
notes.explanation: Light-off alone is not enough: the engine cannot yet keep itself turning.
notes.example: Like pushing a cyclist until they can pedal on their own, not just until they are seated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gas Turbine Engine Starters”, p. 5-8
notes.evidence: To start a gas turbine engine, it is necessary to accelerate the compressor to provide sufficient air to support combustion in the combustion section, or burners. Once ignition and fuel have been introduced and the lite-off has occurred, the starter must continue to assist the engine until the engine reaches a self-sustaining speed.

notes.front: What is an air turbine starter?
notes.back: A starter whose axial flow turbine, driven by compressed air, turns a drive coupling through reduction gears and a clutch.
notes.explanation: Its air comes from a ground air cart, the auxiliary power unit, or cross-bleed from an engine already running.
notes.example: Like a windmill driven by a hose of compressed air, geared to the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starters”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: The typical air turbine starter consists of an axial flow turbine that turns a drive coupling through a reduction gear train and a starter clutch mechanism. The air to operate an air turbine starter is supplied from either a ground-operated air cart, the APU, or a cross-bleed start from an engine already operating.

notes.front: Into which two classifications can reciprocating engine ignition systems be divided?
notes.back: Magneto-ignition systems and electronic FADEC systems.
notes.explanation: Magneto systems are then subclassified again, as single or dual magneto-ignition systems.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: Ignition systems can be divided into two classifications: magneto-ignition systems or electronic Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC) systems for reciprocating engines. Ignition systems can also be subclassified as either single or dual magneto-ignition systems.

notes.front: How does a magneto turn the current in its coil into the high voltage that fires the plug?
notes.back: At the correct time the coil current is stopped, and its magnetic field collapses across a second set of windings.
notes.explanation: The coil current first builds its own field around the windings; that field is what collapses when the current stops.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magneto-Ignition System Operating Principles”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: As current flows through the coil windings, it generates its own magnetic field that surrounds the coil windings. At the correct time, this current flow is stopped and the magnetic field collapses across a second set of windings in the coil and a high-voltage is generated. This is the voltage used to arc across the spark plug gap.

notes.front: A student says an aircraft magneto cannot make a spark unless the aircraft battery is switched on. What do you tell them?
notes.back: B: Wrong. A magneto makes its own current from a permanent magnet, a coil and relative movement.
notes.choices:
A) Right: the battery energises the magnet
B) Wrong: the magneto generates its own current
C) Partly right: the battery is needed only above idle
D) Right: the battery feeds the primary coil
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the magnet is permanent and needs no energising. D is wrong because the rotating magnet induces the primary current. C is wrong because nothing in the magneto depends on the battery at any speed.
notes.explanation: The magneto uses a permanent magnet as its source of energy, so the engine turning it is enough.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magneto-Ignition System Operating Principles”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: The magneto, a special type of engine-driven alternating current (AC) generator, uses a permanent magnet as a source of energy. By the use of a permanent magnet (basic magnetic field), coil of wire (concentrated lengths of conductor), and relative movement of the magnetic field, current is generated in the wire.

notes.front: Which aircraft ignition system is still the most widely used?
notes.back: The high-tension magneto system.
notes.explanation: New lead materials and shielding overcame the high-voltage leakage that once troubled it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-1
notes.evidence: As new materials evolved and shielding was developed, the problems with high-tension magnetos were overcome. The high-tension magneto system is still the most widely used aircraft ignition system.

notes.front: For discussion, into which three circuits is a high-tension magneto divided?
notes.back: The magnetic circuit, the primary electrical circuit and the secondary electrical circuit.
notes.explanation: The division is “for purposes of discussion”: the three work together inside one magneto.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Magneto System Theory of Operation”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: The high-tension magneto system can be divided, for purposes of discussion, into three distinct circuits: magnetic, primary electrical, and secondary electrical circuits.

notes.front: In which of a magneto’s three circuits is the condenser?
notes.back: The primary electrical circuit.
notes.explanation: The primary circuit is made up of the breaker points, the condenser and an insulated coil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The primary electrical circuit consists of a set of breaker contact points, a condenser, and an insulated coil.

notes.front: The neutral position of a magneto’s rotating magnet is {{c1::45°}} from full register; there all the flux is short-circuited and none passes through the coil core.
notes.explanation: As the magnet moves away from full register, more and more flux short-circuits through the pole shoe ends, until at neutral it all does.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Magneto System Theory of Operation”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: As the magnet moves farther from the full register position, more lines of flux are short circuited through the pole shoe ends. Finally, at the neutral position 45° from the full register position, all flux lines are short circuited, and no flux flows through the coil core.

notes.front: A four-pole magneto magnet is turned exactly 90° from a full register position. What flux now passes through the coil core?
notes.back: A: Maximum flux again, but in the opposite direction.
notes.choices:
A) Maximum, in the opposite direction
B) None, because it is in the neutral position
C) Half the maximum, in the same direction
D) Maximum, in the same direction
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because neutral is at 45°, halfway. C is wrong because 90° is a full register position, not a halfway point. D is wrong because the flux reverses as the magnet passes through neutral.
notes.explanation: Every 90° of travel brings another full register position, with the flux reversed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magnetic Circuit”, p. 4-2
notes.evidence: When the magnet is again moved a total of 90°, another full register position is reached with a maximum flux flow in the opposite direction.

notes.front: At about which magnet position do a magneto’s primary breaker points close?
notes.back: At approximately the full register position.
notes.explanation: Closing there completes the primary circuit, so the rotating magnet can induce current in it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: The primary breaker closes at approximately full register position. When the breaker points are closed, the primary electrical circuit is completed and the rotating magnet induces current flow in the primary circuit.

notes.front: Which law explains why current in the primary circuit holds the core flux as the magnet turns?
notes.back: Lenz’s law: an induced current flows so that its magnetism opposes the change that induced it.
notes.explanation: While it flows, the primary current therefore opposes any fall in the magnetic flux in the core.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: While the induced current is flowing in the primary circuit, it opposes any decrease in the magnetic flux in the core. This is in accordance with Lenz’s Law that states: “An induced current always flows in such a direction that its magnetism opposes the motion or the change that induced it.”

notes.front: What happens in the coil core when the breaker points open with the rotor at the E-gap position?
notes.back: The field reverses suddenly, and this high rate of flux change induces the high-voltage pulse in the secondary coil.
notes.explanation: The secondary coil is wound over the primary and insulated from it, so the changing flux cuts across it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: Opening the breaker points stops the flow of current in the primary circuit and allows the magnetic rotor to quickly reverse the field through the coil core. This sudden flux reversal produces a high rate of flux change in the core, that cuts across the secondary coil of the magneto (wound over and insulated from the primary coil),

notes.front: You open a magneto and find the breaker points coarse and crystalline, with black sooty sides. Which component is the likely cause?
notes.back: C: An open-circuited condenser.
notes.choices:
A) Too much oil on the breaker cam
B) Dirt and impurities on the contact surfaces
C) An open-circuited condenser
D) Excessive breaker point spring tension
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because excess cam oil gives smoked, smudged points without these irregularities. B is wrong because dirt causes pitted points. D is wrong because excess spring tension is linked to built-up points.
notes.explanation: Without condenser action an intense arc forms each time the points open, eroding them to this frosted look.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Breaker Point Inspection”, p. 4-40
notes.evidence: This condition results from an open-circuited condenser and is easily recognized by the coarse, crystalline surface and the black “sooty” appearance of the sides of the points.

notes.front: What three events are required to fire a spark plug when its piston is in the prescribed position?
notes.back: The magneto in the E-gap position, the breaker points open, and the distributor correctly aligned.
notes.explanation: The first two belong to the magneto’s own timing; the third sends the spark to the right cylinder.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Primary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-3
notes.evidence: There are three basic events required to fire a spark plug when its piston is in the prescribed position: 1. the magneto must be in the E-gap position, 2. the breaker contact points must be open, and 3. the distributor must be aligned correctly.

notes.front: A magneto’s secondary coil is a winding of approximately {{c1::13,000}} turns of fine, insulated wire.
notes.explanation: One end is grounded to the primary coil or coil core and the other goes to the distributor rotor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The secondary coil is made up of a winding containing approximately 13,000 turns of fine, insulated wire; one end of which is electrically grounded to the primary coil or to the coil core and the other end connected to the distributor rotor.

notes.front: How high can the voltage generated in a high-tension magneto’s secondary circuit be?
notes.back: Often as high as 20,000 volts.
notes.explanation: With other factors constant, the number of turns sets the voltage, and the secondary has many thousands of turns.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The strength of the voltage induced in the secondary windings, when all other factors are constant, is determined by the number of turns of wire. Since most high-tension magnetos have many thousands of turns of wire in the secondary coil windings, a very high-voltage, often as high as 20,000 volts, is generated in the secondary circuit.

notes.front: Two magneto coils are identical except that one secondary winding has more turns. All else being equal, which gives the higher secondary voltage?
notes.back: A: The coil with more secondary turns.
notes.choices:
A) The coil with more turns
B) Both give the same voltage
C) The coil with fewer turns
D) It depends only on the condenser
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong because fewer turns induce less voltage. B is wrong because the turns are the one factor that differs. D is wrong because the handbook ties the induced voltage to the number of turns.
notes.explanation: With other factors constant, the number of turns of wire determines the induced secondary voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The strength of the voltage induced in the secondary windings, when all other factors are constant, is determined by the number of turns of wire.

notes.front: What do the numbers on a distributor block’s electrodes represent?
notes.back: The magneto sparking order, not the engine cylinder numbers.
notes.explanation: Electrode 1 serves the No. 1 cylinder, electrode 2 the second cylinder to fire, and so on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Secondary Electrical Circuit”, p. 4-6
notes.evidence: The distributor numbers represent the magneto sparking order rather than the engine cylinder numbers. The distributor electrode marked “1” is connected to the spark plug in the No. 1 cylinder; distributor electrode marked “2” to the second

notes.front: What is flashover in a magneto?
notes.back: High voltage flashing across a wet insulating surface to ground, or misdirected to the wrong spark plug.
notes.explanation: Moisture is a good conductor, so absorbed moisture creates the stray path; it usually causes misfiring.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Magneto & Distributor Venting”, p. 4-7
notes.evidence: The high-voltage current that normally arcs across the air gaps of the distributor can flash across a wet insulating surface to ground, or the high-voltage current can be misdirected to some spark plug other than the one that should be fired. This condition is called flashover and usually results in cylinder misfiring.

notes.front: What are the two purposes of the ignition harness leads?
notes.back: To carry the high voltage to the spark plug, and to shield the stray magnetic fields around the wires.
notes.explanation: The second job exists because the wires are surrounded by stray fields while they carry high voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness”, p. 4-7
notes.evidence: The ignition harness leads serve a dual purpose. It provides the conductor path for the hightension voltage to the spark plug. It also serves as a shield for stray magnetic fields that surround the wires as they momentarily carry high-voltage current.

notes.front: How does shielding an ignition lead affect the energy needed to fire the plug?
notes.back: It raises lead capacitance, so more magneto primary current is needed to fire the plug.
notes.explanation: The magneto must charge the lead’s capacitance and still have enough energy left to fire the plug.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: The magneto must produce enough energy to charge the capacitance caused by the ignition lead and have enough energy left over to fire the plug. Ignition lead capacitance increases the electrical energy required to provide a spark across the plug gap. More magneto primary current is needed to fire the plug with the shielded lead.

notes.front: A mechanic installing a new ignition lead lets it rest against an exhaust stack and leaves it loose where it vibrates. What is wrong?
notes.back: B: Leads must be routed and clamped to avoid exhaust hot spots and vibration points.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because the silicone coating protects it
B) It must be rerouted and clamped away from exhaust hot spots and vibration points
C) Only the heat matters; vibration does not
D) Only the vibration matters; heat does not
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the handbook still requires correct routing and clamping. D and C are wrong because both hot spots and vibration points must be avoided.
notes.explanation: The lead’s thin silicone coating protects against heat and vibration, but correct routing and clamping are still required.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: a metal mesh, or shielding, covered with a thin silicone rubber coating that prevents damage by engine heat, vibration, or weather. A sectional view of the typical ignition lead is shown in Figure 4-12. Ignition leads must be routed and clamped correctly to avoid hot spots on the exhaust and vibration points

notes.front: In what way is an ignition switch unlike almost every other switch?
notes.back: In the off position it completes a circuit to ground; other switches normally open the circuit when off.
notes.explanation: Off is a closed circuit here, the reverse of ordinary switch logic.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switches”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: The ignition switch is different in at least one respect from all other types of switches: when the ignition switch is in the off position, a circuit is completed through the switch to ground. In other electrical switches, the off position normally breaks or opens the circuit.

notes.front: Why does a closed (off) ignition switch stop the magneto sparking?
notes.back: Primary current is not stopped when the points open, so there is no sudden collapse of the primary field.
notes.explanation: The closed switch gives the primary current another path to ground that the points cannot interrupt.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switches”, p. 4-9
notes.evidence: Figure 4-15 shows that the primary current is not interrupted when the breaker contacts open since there is still a path to ground through the closed, or off, ignition switch. Since primary current is not stopped when the contact points open, there can be no sudden collapse of the primary coil flux field

notes.front: A P-lead has broken between a magneto and the ignition switch. With the switch set to off, what state is that magneto in?
notes.back: A: Still live: it cannot be switched off.
notes.choices:
A) Live, because its P-lead can no longer be grounded
B) Off, because the switch is set to off
C) Off, because a broken wire opens the circuit
D) Live only above idle speed
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the switch works through the P-lead it can no longer reach. C is wrong because opening the P-lead leaves the magneto running, not stopped. D is wrong because nothing limits the danger to high speeds.
notes.explanation: A magneto is turned off only by grounding its P-lead, and a broken lead cannot be grounded by the switch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Glossary: P-lead”, p. G-20
notes.evidence: P-lead. Primary lead. The wire that connects the primary winding of a magneto to the ignition switch. The magneto is turned off by grounding its P-lead.

notes.front: Which three ignition risks does the Airman Certification Standards list for Powerplant subject H?
notes.back: Advanced and retarded timing; maintenance on capacitor discharge ignition; working near a reciprocating engine with an ungrounded magneto.
notes.explanation: Each is a hazard to the engine or to people, which is why the standards test risk management here.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant ACS (FAA-S-ACS-1), III.H “Ignition and Starting Systems: Risk Management”
notes.evidence: AM.III.H.R1 Advanced and retarded ignition timing (piston engine). AM.III.H.R2 Maintenance on engines with capacitor discharge ignition systems. AM.III.H.R3 Working around reciprocating engines with an ungrounded magneto.

notes.front: Single magneto versus dual magneto: what is inside each housing?
notes.back: Single: one magneto with distributor, breaker, magnet and coil. Dual: two magnetos sharing one magnet and cam, each with own points, coil and distributor.
notes.explanation: The dual design saves a housing and a rotating magnet by feeding two complete magnetos from one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Single & Dual High-Tension System Magnetos”, p. 4-10
notes.evidence: The single magneto design incorporates the distributor in the housing with the magneto breaker assembly, rotating magnet, and coil. [Figure 4-17] The dual magneto incorporates two magnetos contained in a single housing. One rotating magnet and a cam are common to two sets of breaker points and coils. Two separate distributor units are mounted in the magneto.

notes.front: In a low-tension magneto system, where is the voltage raised to spark level?
notes.back: In a transformer coil near each spark plug, which feeds the plug through very short high-tension leads.
notes.explanation: The magneto itself generates only low voltage, which travels to the transformer’s primary winding.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High- & Low-Tension Magneto Systems”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: In the low-tension system, low-voltage is generated in the magneto and flows to the primary winding of a transformer coil located near the spark plug. There, the voltage is increased to high by transformer action and conducted to the spark plug by very short high-tension leads.

notes.front: Why does a low-tension system virtually eliminate flashover?
notes.back: A brush-type distributor removes the distributor air gaps, and high voltage exists only in short leads from transformer to plug.
notes.explanation: Flashover needs high voltage and a gap to jump; this design removes both from most of the system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High- & Low-Tension Magneto Systems”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: The low-tension system virtually eliminates flashover in both the distributor and the harness because the air gaps within the distributor have been eliminated by the use of a brush-type distributor, and high-voltage is present only in short leads between the transformer and spark plug.

notes.front: High-tension versus low-tension magneto system: where is high voltage present?
notes.back: High-tension: from the magneto through the whole harness to the plug. Low-tension: only in short leads from each plug’s transformer.
notes.explanation: Low-tension systems see limited use now because good lead materials and shielding exist and a coil per plug adds cost.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High- & Low-Tension Magneto Systems”, p. 4-12
notes.evidence: Low-tension ignition systems have limited use in modern aircraft because of the excellent materials and shielding available to construct hightension ignition leads and the added cost of a coil for each spark plug with the low-tension system.

notes.front: An old engine’s magneto sends low voltage to a coil mounted beside each spark plug. Which kind of ignition system is it?
notes.back: C: A low-tension magneto system.
notes.choices:
A) A high-tension magneto system
B) A battery-ignition system
C) A low-tension magneto system
D) A capacitor discharge system
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because a high-tension magneto sends high voltage down the leads. B is wrong because here a magneto, not a battery, generates the current. D is wrong because capacitor discharge ignition is the turbine system.
notes.explanation: Generating low voltage and raising it at a transformer near each plug is what defines the low-tension system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High- & Low-Tension Magneto Systems”, p. 4-11
notes.evidence: In the low-tension system, low-voltage is generated in the magneto and flows to the primary winding of a transformer coil located near the spark plug.

notes.front: Besides crankshaft speed and top dead centre position, which two induction conditions does a reciprocating-engine FADEC monitor?
notes.back: Induction manifold pressure and induction air temperature.
notes.explanation: From these it adjusts the fuel-to-air ratio and ignition timing for the power setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-14
notes.evidence: FADEC monitors engine operating conditions (crankshaft speed, top dead center position, the induction manifold pressure, and the induction air temperature) and then automatically adjusts the fuel-to-air ratio mixture and ignition timing accordingly for any given power setting to attain optimum engine performance.

notes.front: Which two items do engines equipped with FADEC not need?
notes.back: Magnetos and manual mixture control.
notes.explanation: The system itself sets mixture and ignition timing for every power setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “FADEC System Description”, p. 4-14
notes.evidence: and then automatically adjusts the fuel-to-air ratio mixture and ignition timing accordingly for any given power setting to attain optimum engine performance. As a result, engines equipped with FADEC require neither magnetos nor manual mixture control.

notes.front: If one control channel inside a FADEC ECU fails, what happens?
notes.back: The other channel in the same ECU runs both its own cylinder and the opposing cylinder as backup.
notes.explanation: The channels share no electronic components and run on separate power supplies, so one can survive the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Electronic Control Unit (ECU)”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: The control channels are independent, and there are no shared electronic components within one ECU. They also operate on independent and separate power supplies. However, if one control channel fails, the other control channel in the pair within the same ECU is capable of operating both its assigned cylinder and the other opposing engine cylinder as backup control

notes.front: A mechanic plans to check ignition timing on a PowerLink FADEC engine with a timing light, as on a magneto engine. What should you tell them?
notes.back: B: It cannot be done that way: the ECUs set the timing and it cannot be adjusted by hand.
notes.choices:
A) Go ahead, then adjust at the magneto flange
B) Timing is set by the ECUs and cannot be adjusted manually
C) Go ahead, then adjust the ECU mounting
D) Time only the left bank of cylinders
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because FADEC engines have no magnetos. C is wrong because timing is not set mechanically on this system. D is wrong because no cylinder’s timing can be set manually.
notes.explanation: On this system the control units establish ignition timing, which varies with engine load.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “PowerLink Ignition System”, p. 4-16
notes.evidence: Note: Engine ignition timing is established by the ECUs and cannot be manually adjusted.

notes.front: Why is a magneto’s output low while the engine is being cranked?
notes.back: Its voltage depends on magnet speed, and during cranking the magnet turns at only about 80 rpm.
notes.explanation: Magnet strength and coil turns are fixed, so rotation speed is the only variable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Auxiliary Ignition Units”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: Since the strength of the rotating magnet and the number of turns in the coil are constant factors in magneto ignition systems, the voltage produced depends upon the speed at which the rotating magnet is turned. When the engine is being cranked for starting, the magnet is rotated at about 80 rpm.

notes.front: To which magneto are auxiliary ignition units ordinarily connected?
notes.back: The left magneto, with the unit energised by the battery.
notes.explanation: They exist to give a high ignition voltage when the magneto alone turns too slowly to make one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Auxiliary Ignition Units”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: To facilitate engine starting, an auxiliary device is connected to the magneto to provide a high ignition voltage. Ordinarily, such auxiliary ignition units are energized by the battery and connected to the left magneto.

notes.front: Why must the ignition be retarded during starting?
notes.back: To prevent kickback, with the piston trying to turn the engine opposite to normal rotation.
notes.explanation: The engine is turning very slowly compared with normal speed during the starting cycle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Auxiliary Ignition Units”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: During the starting cycle, the engine is turning very slowly compared to normal speed. The ignition must be retarded or moved back to prevent kickback of the piston trying to

notes.front: A mechanic says a magneto gives just as strong a spark during slow cranking as in cruise, so no starting aid is needed. What is the flaw?
notes.back: B: At cranking speed the magnet turns slowly, so the induced voltage may be too low to jump the plug gap.
notes.choices:
A) None: magneto voltage does not depend on speed
B) Slow magnet rotation gives too low a voltage to spark reliably
C) The condenser is disconnected during cranking
D) The spark plugs are cold, not the magneto
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because with magnet and coil fixed, voltage depends on magnet speed. C is wrong because the condenser stays in the primary circuit. D is wrong because the problem named in the handbook is the low induced voltage.
notes.explanation: That is why an auxiliary device is connected to the magneto to give a high ignition voltage for starting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Auxiliary Ignition Units”, p. 4-17
notes.evidence: Since the value of the induced voltage is so low, a spark may not jump the spark plug gap. To facilitate engine starting, an auxiliary device is connected to the magneto to provide a high ignition voltage.

notes.front: What are the two functions of an impulse coupling?
notes.back: To spin the magneto fast enough for a good spark, and to retard the spark during the start cycle.
notes.explanation: The released spring gives the magnet a quick twist, equivalent to high-speed rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Impulse Coupling”, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: This, being equivalent to high-speed magneto rotation, produces a spark that jumps the gap at the spark plug electrodes. The impulse coupling has two functions: rotating the magneto fast enough to produce a good spark and retarding the timing of the spark during the start cycle.

notes.front: How can you tell an engine has an impulse coupling when turning it at cranking speed?
notes.back: A sharp clicking noise as the crankshaft passes top centre on each cylinder.
notes.explanation: The click is the coupling releasing and snapping the magneto forward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Impulse Coupling”, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: The presence of an impulse coupling is identified by a sharp clicking noise as the crankshaft is turned at starter cranking speed past top center on each cylinder.

notes.front: On a very cold morning an engine with an impulse coupling cranks normally but gives no starting spark, and none of the usual clicks. What is a likely cause?
notes.back: B: Congealed oil or sludge on the flyweights, stopping them engaging the stop pins.
notes.choices:
A) The condenser is too cold to charge
B) Congealed oil or sludge on the flyweights
C) The distributor rotor has frozen to the block
D) The spark plugs have the wrong heat range
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the handbook names no cold-weather condenser fault. D is wrong because plug heat range would not stop the clicking. C is wrong because the missing clicks point to the coupling, not the distributor.
notes.explanation: If the flyweights cannot engage the stop pins, the coupling never winds and releases, so no starting spark is made.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Impulse Coupling”, p. 4-20
notes.evidence: Congealed oil or sludge on the flyweights during cold weather may produce the same results. This prevents the flyweight weights from engaging the stop pins, which results in no starting spark being produced.

notes.front: Starting vibrator versus booster coil: which one produces the high ignition voltage itself?
notes.back: The booster coil. The starting vibrator only turns battery current into pulsating current for the magneto’s primary coil.
notes.explanation: With the vibrator, the magneto’s own coils still make the high voltage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Retard Breaker Vibrator”, p. 4-21
notes.evidence: The starting vibrator, unlike the booster coil, does not produce the high ignition voltage within itself. The function of this starting vibrator is to change the DC of the battery into a pulsating DC and deliver it to the primary coil of the magneto.

notes.front: Which starting aid delivers several sparks at the spark plug electrodes during starting rather than one?
notes.back: D: The shower of sparks (starting vibrator).
notes.choices:
A) The impulse coupling
B) A flange-mounted magneto
C) The P-lead
D) The shower of sparks
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because an impulse coupling gives only one spark per firing cycle. B is wrong because mounting has nothing to do with spark count. C is wrong because the P-lead only switches the magneto off.
notes.explanation: It was developed to give more spark power while starting by providing several sparks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Retard Breaker Vibrator”, p. 4-21
notes.evidence: To provide for more spark power during the starting cycle, the shower of sparks system was developed, which provides several sparks at the spark plug electrodes during starting.

notes.front: At 2,100 rpm, one cylinder’s spark plug must fire about {{c1::17}} separate high-voltage sparks each second.
notes.explanation: So many sparks look like a continuous spark across the electrodes at over 3,000 °F.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: A cylinder of an engine operating at 2,100 rpm must produce approximately 17 separate and distinct high-voltage sparks that bridge the air gap of a single spark plug each second. This would appear as a continuous spark across the spark plug electrodes at temperatures of over 3,000 °F.

notes.front: What gas pressure and electrical pressure can a spark plug face?
notes.back: Gas pressures as high as 2,000 psi and electrical pressure as high as 20,000 volts.
notes.explanation: The engine loses power if even one spark fails, so the plug must work reliably under these extremes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: At the same time, the spark plug is subjected to gas pressures as high as 2,000 pounds per square inch (psi) and electrical pressure as high as 20,000 volts. Given the extremes that spark plugs must operate under, and the fact that the engine loses power if one spark does not occur correctly

notes.front: What is a spark plug’s insulator made of?
notes.back: Aluminium oxide ceramic.
notes.explanation: Besides insulating, the ceramic core carries heat from its nose to the cylinder.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-24
notes.evidence: In addition to affording electrical insulation, the ceramic insulator core also transfers heat from the ceramic tip, or nose, to the cylinder. The insulator is made from aluminum oxide ceramic having excellent dielectric strength, high mechanical strength, and thermal conductivity.

notes.front: An engine runs rough. New spark plugs cure it, but the roughness returns a few hours later. What is the best next step?
notes.back: C: Look for the real cause in another system, such as the carburettor, fuel distribution or primer.
notes.choices:
A) Replace the plugs again at shorter intervals
B) Fit colder plugs
C) Look for the real cause in another engine system
D) Replace both magnetos
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because nothing suggests a heat range problem. A is wrong because repeated plug changes only mask the fault. D is wrong because the evidence points away from ignition, not towards the magnetos.
notes.explanation: Faults elsewhere show the same symptoms as faulty ignition, and a plug change only hides them for a while.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition System Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: Spark plugs are often diagnosed as being faulty when the real malfunction exists in a different system. Malfunctioning of the carburetor, poor fuel distribution, too much valve overlap, leaking primer system, or poor idle speed and mixture settings show symptoms that are the same as those for faulty ignition.

notes.front: What is the principal factor in a spark plug’s heat range?
notes.back: The length of the insulator nose core.
notes.explanation: A long nose makes a long heat path (a hot plug); a short one moves heat quickly to the cylinder head (a cold plug).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: The length of the nose core is the principal factor in establishing the plug’s heat range. [Figure 4-41] Hot plugs have a long insulator nose that creates a long heat transfer path; cold plugs have a relatively short insulator to provide a rapid transfer of heat to the cylinder head.

notes.front: How should a spark plug ideally behave across different engine loads?
notes.back: As hot as possible at slow speeds and light loads, and as cool as possible at cruise and takeoff power.
notes.explanation: Flight imposes different loads on the engine, so the plug cannot be designed for one speed only.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: Because flight demands impose different loads on the engine, spark plugs must be designed to operate as hot as possible at slow speeds and light loads, and as cool as possible at cruise and takeoff power.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-1B, what heat range of plug does an engine that runs hot need?
notes.back: A relatively cold plug; an engine that runs cool needs a relatively hot one.
notes.explanation: A hot plug in a hot-running engine overheats at the tip and causes pre-ignition.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, para. 8-15 “Spark Plugs”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: Fundamentally, an engine which runs hot requires a relatively cold spark plug, whereas an engine which runs cool requires a relatively hot spark plug. If a hot spark plug is installed in an engine which runs hot, the spark plug tip will be overheated and cause pre-ignition.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-1B, above what core nose temperature is pre-ignition likely, and below what tip temperature is carbon fouling likely?
notes.back: Pre-ignition above 1,630 °F (888 °C); carbon fouling below about 800 °F (427 °C).
notes.explanation: A plug must work between these limits, which is why plugs come in several heat ranges.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, para. 8-15 “Spark Plugs”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: Pre-ignition is likely to occur if surface areas in the combustion chamber exceed critical limits or if the spark plug core nose temperature exceeds 1,630 ºF (888 ºC). However, fouling or short circuiting of the plug due to carbon deposits is likely to occur if the insulator tip temperature drops below approximately 800 ºF (427 ºC).

notes.front: A hot spark plug is fitted to an engine that runs hot. What result does AC 43.13-1B predict?
notes.back: B: The plug tip overheats and causes pre-ignition.
notes.choices:
A) Carbon fouling of the tip
B) Pre-ignition from an overheated tip
C) Lead fouling at cruise
D) No effect, since heat range affects only starting
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because carbon fouling comes from a cold plug in a cool-running engine. C is wrong because lead fouling comes from leaded fuel, not heat range choice. D is wrong because heat range governs plug temperature in all operation.
notes.explanation: An engine that runs hot needs a relatively cold plug to carry heat away quickly.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, para. 8-15 “Spark Plugs”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: If a hot spark plug is installed in an engine which runs hot, the spark plug tip will be overheated and cause pre-ignition.

notes.front: What can happen if a spark plug with too long a reach is fitted?
notes.back: Seizure or improper combustion; in extreme cases the plug may hit a piston or valve and damage the engine.
notes.explanation: Reach decides where the electrode end sits in the cylinder, so the wrong reach puts it in the wrong place.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: Spark plug seizure and/or improper combustion within the cylinder can occur if a plug with the wrong reach is used. In extreme cases, if the reach is too long, the plug may contact a piston or valve and damage the engine.

notes.front: A spark plug with a longer reach than approved is fitted, and its threads project into the combustion chamber. Which problem can follow?
notes.back: A: Carbon sticks to the exposed threads, making the plug almost impossible to remove, and can cause pre-ignition.
notes.choices:
A) Carbon on the threads, a seized plug and possible pre-ignition
B) Only a slightly lower heat range
C) Nothing, if the torque is correct
D) Lead fouling of the electrodes
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong because correct torque does not stop carbon forming on exposed threads. B is wrong because reach is a separate property from heat range. D is wrong because lead fouling comes from leaded fuel, not reach.
notes.explanation: Heat of combustion can turn some of that carbon into an ignition source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plugs”, p. 4-25
notes.evidence: If the plug threads are too long, they extend into the combustion chamber and carbon adheres to the threads making it almost impossible to remove the plug. This can also be a source of pre-ignition. Heat of combustion can make some of the carbon a source for ignition, which can ignite the air-fuel mixture prematurely.

notes.front: Timing a magneto, a mechanic reads the built-in timing mark while looking at it from one side. What is the problem?
notes.back: C: Sighting at an angle gives an error in positioning the crankshaft; sight straight across the mark.
notes.choices:
A) The error matters only on radial engines
B) None, provided the light is good
C) Sighting at an angle mispositions the crankshaft
D) Only the distributor will be out of time
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the error comes from the viewing angle, not the light. A is wrong because the handbook gives no such exception. D is wrong because the error is in crankshaft position, which affects the whole timing.
notes.explanation: Built-in marks must be sighted straight across the stationary pointer or mark.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Built-In Engine Timing Reference Marks”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: In using built-in timing marks to position the crankshaft, be sure to sight straight across the stationary pointer or mark on the nose section, the propeller shaft, crankshaft flange, or bell gear. [Figure 4-45] Sighting at an angle results in an error in positioning the crankshaft.

notes.front: Why should engine timing always be taken with movement in the direction of rotation?
notes.back: Gear backlash varies between installations because there is clearance between the gear teeth.
notes.explanation: Approaching the mark from the same direction takes up that clearance consistently.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Built-In Engine Timing Reference Marks”, p. 4-27
notes.evidence: The amount of gear backlash in any system of gears varies between installations because there is clearance between the gear teeth. Always take timing when reading, or stop movement of the engine for timing set up, in the direction of rotation.

notes.front: With a typical timing light connected to closed breaker points, why do its lights stay off?
notes.back: Most current flows through the closed points, not the transformers; when the points open, the lights glow.
notes.explanation: Some models work the other way round, with the light going out when the points open.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing Lights”, p. 4-28
notes.evidence: If the points are closed, most of the current flows through the breaker points and not through the transformers, and the lights do not come on. If the points are open, the current flows through the transformer and the lights glow. Some models of timing lights operate in the reverse manner (i.e., the light goes out when the points open).

notes.front: A timing light is connected to both magnetos of an installed ignition system, but its lights never change as the propeller is turned. The ignition switch is at off. What is wrong?
notes.back: D: The ignition switch must be turned to both, or the lights do not show point opening.
notes.choices:
A) The timing light’s ground lead is on the magneto case
B) The propeller is being turned the wrong way
C) The breaker points are welded shut
D) The ignition switch is not at both
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because a ground lead on the magneto is not what keeps the lights from changing; the switch at off is. C is wrong because the switch position alone explains the symptom. B is wrong because turning direction would not stop the lights changing.
notes.explanation: In the off position the switch grounds the primary circuits, so the points’ opening cannot show.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing the High-tension Magneto to the Engine”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: When using the timing light to check a magneto in a complete ignition system installed on the aircraft, the ignition switch for the engine must be turned to both. Otherwise, the lights do not indicate breaker point opening.

notes.front: For correct ignition timing, as the magnet reaches E-gap the breaker points must be just opening on the {{c1::No. 1 cam lobe}}.
notes.explanation: At the same instant the distributor finger must line up with the electrode serving the No. 1 cylinder.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition System Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: The rotating magnet of the magneto must be in the E-gap position. 3. The breaker points must be just opening on the No. 1 cam lobe. 4. The distributor finger must be aligned with the electrode serving the No. 1 cylinder.
