notes.front: What happens if ignition occurs too early?
notes.back: The rising piston meets the full force of combustion: power loss, overheating, and possible detonation and pre-ignition.
notes.explanation: Early timing means ignition before the optimum crankshaft position is reached.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition System Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: If ignition occurs too early, the piston rising in the cylinder is opposed by the full force of combustion. This condition results in a loss of engine power, overheating, and possible detonation and pre-ignition.

notes.front: After magneto work, an engine loses power, runs hot and shows signs of detonation. Which timing error best fits?
notes.back: D: Ignition too early (too far advanced).
notes.choices:
A) Ignition too late
B) Staggered timing on one magneto
C) Timing exactly correct, so the fault is elsewhere
D) Ignition too early
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because late ignition causes power loss and a larger throttle opening, not detonation. B is wrong because staggered timing is a deliberate design on some early engines. C is wrong because these are the handbook’s signs of early timing.
notes.explanation: Too-early ignition makes the rising piston fight the full force of combustion, causing these symptoms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition System Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: If ignition occurs too early, the piston rising in the cylinder is opposed by the full force of combustion. This condition results in a loss of engine power, overheating, and possible detonation and pre-ignition.

notes.front: After magneto work, an engine needs a wider throttle opening than before to hold the same propeller load, with no overheating. Which timing error best fits?
notes.back: A: Ignition too late (retarded).
notes.choices:
A) Ignition too late
B) An open P-lead
C) Spark plugs with too long a reach
D) Ignition too early
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong because early ignition brings overheating and possible detonation. B is wrong because an open P-lead stops a magneto being switched off; it does not change timing. C is wrong because wrong reach is not linked to this symptom.
notes.explanation: Late ignition leaves too little time to burn the charge, so power drops and more throttle is needed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Ignition System Maintenance & Inspection”, p. 4-26
notes.evidence: If it occurs too late, not enough time is allowed to consume the air-fuel charge, and combustion is incomplete. As a result, the engine loses power and requires a greater throttle opening to carry a given propeller load.

notes.front: Bench-checking a magneto, you lay a straightedge along the step on the breaker cam and it lines up with the housing rim marks, but the points are still firmly closed. What does this tell you?
notes.back: A: The points need adjusting: at this E-gap position they should just be beginning to open.
notes.choices:
A) The points need adjusting to open at this position
B) All is correct: the points open later, at full register
C) The rotor is at neutral, so turn it back
D) The condenser needs replacing
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the points close, not open, near full register. C is wrong because the aligned step shows the E-gap position, not neutral. D is wrong because point opening is set by adjustment.
notes.explanation: The step and rim marks show the rotor is at E-gap, where the points should just begin to open.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Checking the Internal Timing of a Magneto”, p. 4-29
notes.evidence: When a straightedge is laid along this step and it coincides with the timing marks on the rim of the breaker housing, the magneto rotor is then in the E-gap position, and the breaker contact points should just begin to open.

notes.front: Bench timing an S-200 magneto, you measure 0.026 inch between the points at the high point of the cam lobe. What next?
notes.back: C: It is outside 0.018 ± 0.006 inch, so adjust the points, then recheck and readjust the timing.
notes.choices:
A) Replace the magneto
B) Accept it: it is within limits
C) Adjust the points, then recheck the timing
D) Adjust the points but leave the timing
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the upper limit is 0.024 inch. A is wrong because points are adjusted first, and replaced only if they cannot be set to open on time. D is wrong because the timing must be rechecked after adjusting the points.
notes.explanation: The limit tops out at 0.024 inch, and any point adjustment means the breaker opening must be rechecked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Magneto E-Gap Setting (Bench Timing)”, p. 4-29
notes.evidence: This clearance must be 0.018 inch ± 0.006 inch [0.46 millimeter (mm) ± 0.15 mm]. If the breaker point clearance is not within these limits, the points must be adjusted for correct setting. It is then necessary to recheck and readjust the timing for breaker opening.

notes.front: What two factors must be considered when replacing magnetos on an engine?
notes.back: The magneto’s internal timing, including point adjustment, and the crankshaft position at which the spark occurs.
notes.explanation: Correct internal timing is needed to get the maximum potential voltage from the magneto.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing the High-tension Magneto to the Engine”, p. 4-30
notes.evidence: When replacing magnetos on aircraft engines, two factors must be considered: 1. The internal timing of the magneto, including breaker point adjustment, which must be correct to obtain maximum potential voltage from the magneto. 2. The engine crankshaft position where the spark occurs.

notes.front: Where in its slotted mounting flange should a magneto first be installed when timing it to the engine?
notes.back: In the middle of the slots.
notes.explanation: That leaves room either way for fine timing of the magneto to the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing the High-tension Magneto to the Engine”, p. 4-30
notes.evidence: It should be installed in the middle of its slotted flange to allow for fine timing of the magneto to the engine.

notes.front: Timing a magneto to the engine, you find the flange slots do not let it move far enough for the points to open at the No. 1 firing position. What do you do?
notes.back: B: Move the magneto out far enough to turn its drive shaft, reinstall it, and repeat the point-opening check.
notes.choices:
A) Elongate the flange slots with a file
B) Pull the magneto out, turn its drive shaft, refit and recheck
C) Leave it as close as the slots allow
D) Adjust the breaker points to open early instead
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the handbook’s method is to reposition the drive, not modify the flange. D is wrong because that would upset the internal timing. C is wrong because the points must open at the firing position.
notes.explanation: The flange slots allow only limited adjustment, so a larger correction is made at the drive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Timing the High-tension Magneto to the Engine”, p. 4-30
notes.evidence: If the slots in the mounting flange of the magneto do not permit sufficient movement to effect breaker point opening for the No. 1 cylinder, move the magneto out of position far enough to permit turning the magneto drive shaft. Then, install the magneto in position again and repeat the previous check for point opening.

notes.front: In a typical magneto check, what rpm drop is generally seen on each magneto?
notes.back: About 25–75 rpm, and it should be even for both magnetos.
notes.explanation: Running on one magneto burns the charge less efficiently than two; always check the aircraft manual for figures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Performing Ignition System Checks”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: The magneto drop should be even for both magnetos and is generally in the area of a 25–75 rpm drop for each magneto. Always refer to the aircraft operating manual for specific information. This rpm drop is because operating on one magneto combustion is not as efficient as it is with two magnetos providing sparks in the cylinder.

notes.front: During run-up the left magneto drops 50 rpm and the right drops 180 rpm, against a manual limit of 75. What do you do?
notes.back: B: Check the ignition system; the fault can be isolated by running on the right magneto.
notes.choices:
A) Accept it: any drop under 200 rpm is normal
B) Check the ignition system, isolating the fault on the right magneto
C) Replace both magnetos at once
D) Repeat the check at a higher rpm until it passes
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the drop is uneven and over the manual limit. C is wrong because the check tests leads and plugs as well, so the fault may not be a magneto at all. D is wrong because changing the rpm hides the fault instead of finding it.
notes.explanation: The drop should be even and within limits, and a single high-drop magneto points to where to look.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Performing Ignition System Checks”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: If either magneto has excessive rpm drop while operating by itself, the ignition system needs to be checked for problems. If only one magneto has a high magneto drop, the problem can be isolated and corrected by operating on that magneto.

notes.front: At what engine speed is the ignition switch check usually made?
notes.back: At 700 rpm, or the lowest possible speed on engines that do not idle that low.
notes.explanation: The check confirms that all magneto ground leads are electrically grounded.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switch Check”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: The ignition switch check is performed to see that all magneto ground leads are electrically grounded. The ignition switch check is usually made at 700 rpm. On those aircraft engine installations that do not idle at this low rpm, set the engine speed to the lowest possible to perform this check.

notes.front: During the ignition switch check, how long should the switch be left at off?
notes.back: Only until a 200–300 rpm drop is seen; then return it to both as rapidly as possible.
notes.explanation: Returning it quickly removes the chance of afterfire and backfire when the switch goes back to both.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switch Check”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: The engine should completely quit firing. After a drop of 200–300 rpm is observed, return the switch to the both position as rapidly as possible. Do this quickly to eliminate the possibility of afterfire and backfire when the ignition switch is returned to both.

notes.front: If the engine stops during the ignition switch check because the switch was not returned in time, what should you do?
notes.back: Leave the switch off, put the mixture in idle cut-off, and let the engine rest a short time before restarting.
notes.explanation: Idle cut-off avoids loading the cylinders and exhaust system with raw fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switch Check”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: In this case, leave the ignition switch in the off position and place the mixture control in the idle-cutoff position to avoid overloading the cylinders and exhaust system with raw fuel. When the engine has completely stopped, allow it to remain inoperative for a short time before restarting.

notes.front: At 700 rpm you turn the ignition switch to off and the engine keeps running smoothly. After shutdown, a colleague wants to pull the propeller through by hand. What do you do?
notes.back: D: Stop them: the P-lead is open, a magneto is live, and the engine could start. Correct the fault first.
notes.choices:
A) Allow it if the mixture is at idle cut-off
B) Allow it, as the switch is now off
C) Allow it once the engine has cooled
D) Stop them: a magneto is live because a P-lead is open
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the switch cannot ground an open P-lead. C is wrong because a live magneto does not depend on engine temperature. A is wrong because an engine can still fire on residual fuel with a live magneto.
notes.explanation: An open P-lead means a magneto is not shut off, and turning the propeller can then cause injury or death.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Switch Check”, p. 4-31
notes.evidence: If the engine does not cease firing in the off position, the magneto ground lead, more commonly referred to as the P lead, is open, and the trouble must be corrected. This means that one or more of the magnetos are not being shut off even when the ignition switch is in the off position.

notes.front: Why should bends be avoided when installing ignition leads?
notes.back: Weak points may develop in the insulation, through which high-tension current can leak.
notes.explanation: Leakage through insulation is a lead failure in itself, whatever caused the weak point.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Maintenance & Inspection of Ignition Leads”, p. 4-32
notes.evidence: When installing the leads, you should avoid bends because weak points may develop in the insulation through which high-tension current can leak.

notes.front: In a lead insulation test, the tester’s indicator lamp flashes but its gap does not fire. What does this tell you about the lead?
notes.back: It is defective and must be replaced: the pulse leaked through the wire instead of reaching the gap.
notes.explanation: The flash shows a high-voltage impulse was sent out; a pulse that never arrives has leaked away.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Maintenance & Inspection of Ignition Leads”, p. 4-32
notes.evidence: If the indicator lamp flashes and the gap fails to fire, the lead under test is defective and must be replaced. The indicator lamp flashes to show that a high-voltage impulse was sent out. If it fails to pass through the tester, then the electrical pulse leaked through the wire showing it to be defective.

notes.front: When should a complete ignition harness be replaced, rather than individual leads?
notes.back: Only when the manifold shielding is damaged, or so many leads are faulty that replacing the harness is more practical.
notes.explanation: Extensive harness tests should come before replacing any harness to cure an engine fault.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Replacement of Ignition Harness”, p. 4-33
notes.evidence: Replace a complete ignition harness only when the shielding of the manifold is damaged or when the number of defective leads makes it more practical to replace the harness than to replace the individual leads.

notes.front: According to the handbook, what is the more serious effect when a cylinder fires on only one plug because of a dead lead?
notes.back: The longer burning time overheats the cylinder, causing detonation, possible pre-ignition and perhaps permanent damage.
notes.explanation: The power lost from one cylinder is minor by comparison.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness Maintenance”, p. 4-41
notes.evidence: However, the power loss from a single cylinder becomes a minor factor when the effects of a longer burning time is considered. A longer burning time overheats the affected cylinder, causing detonation, possible pre-ignition, and perhaps permanent damage to the cylinder.

notes.front: What does the electrical harness test measure?
notes.back: Current leakage between each lead and the grounded manifold at a set applied voltage, compared with specifications.
notes.explanation: Insulation slowly deteriorates with age, letting more current leak, so the leakage figure shows serviceability.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Harness Testing”, p. 4-42
notes.evidence: This test involves application of a definite voltage to each lead, and then measurement with a very sensitive meter of the amount of current leakage between the lead and the grounded harness manifold. This reading, when compared with known specifications, becomes a guide to the condition or serviceability of the cable.

notes.front: An engine runs smoothly in cruise but misfires on takeoff, when manifold pressure is high. One harness lead has scuffed insulation. How does this fit?
notes.back: D: The scuffed lead leaks more than normal, and its plug can be lost at high manifold pressure.
notes.choices:
A) It does not: scuffed insulation only matters once fully broken
B) High manifold pressure lowers gap resistance, so it must be the plug
C) The symptom points to a timing error instead
D) The lead leaks more than normal and loses its plug at high manifold pressure
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because partial damage already raises leakage. C is wrong because a timing error would not appear only at high manifold pressure. B is wrong because higher manifold pressure raises, not lowers, gap resistance.
notes.explanation: High manifold pressure raises gap resistance, pushing the spark to leak through the weakened insulation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “High-Tension Ignition Harness Faults”, p. 4-42
notes.evidence: Fault B illustrates a cable with a portion of its insulation scuffed away. Although the insulation is not completely broken down, more than normal leakage exists, and the spark plug to which this cable is connected may be lost during takeoff when the manifold pressure is quite high.

notes.front: What faults are almost always behind carbon fouling from fuel?
notes.back: An improper idle mixture, a leaking primer, or carburettor faults making the idle mixture too rich.
notes.explanation: All of them put more fuel into the idle range than can burn.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Carbon Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-33
notes.evidence: These difficulties are almost invariably associated with an improper idle mixture adjustment, a leaking primer, or carburetor malfunctions that cause too rich a mixture in the idle range.

notes.front: What is added to leaded aviation fuel to minimise lead deposits?
notes.back: Ethylene dibromide, a scavenging agent.
notes.explanation: It combines with the lead during combustion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Lead Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-34
notes.evidence: To minimize the formation of lead deposits, ethylene dibromide is added to the fuel as a scavenging agent that combines with the lead during combustion.

notes.front: How have manufacturers partly overcome gap erosion?
notes.back: With a hermetically sealed resistor in the centre electrode.
notes.explanation: The added resistance cuts peak current at the instant of firing, which helps prevent electrode metal breaking down.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gap Erosion of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: Spark plug manufacturers have partially overcome the problem of gap erosion by using a hermetically sealed resistor in the center electrode of spark plugs. This added resistance in the high-tension circuit reduces the peak current at the instant of firing. This reduced current flow helps prevent metal disintegration in the electrodes.

notes.front: A plug from a rough-idling engine is covered in black soot; the exhaust smokes black at idle and rpm rises when the idle mixture is leaned. Which fouling is this?
notes.back: B: Carbon fouling from a rich idle mixture.
notes.choices:
A) Oil fouling
B) Carbon fouling
C) Lead fouling
D) Graphite fouling
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because oil fouling leaves the plug wet with lubricating oil. C is wrong because lead fouling comes from leaded fuel deposits. D is wrong because graphite fouling comes from antiseize compound on the electrodes.
notes.explanation: Soot, black smoke and an rpm rise on leaning are how a rich idle mixture is detected.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Carbon Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-33
notes.evidence: A rich air-fuel mixture is detected by soot or black smoke coming from the exhaust and by an increase in rpm when the idling air-fuel mixture is leaned to best power.

notes.front: An engine with a correct idle mixture has one plug that is wet with lubricating oil after starting, and white fumes clear from the exhaust once rpm rises. Which fouling is this?
notes.back: B: Oil fouling.
notes.choices:
A) Carbon fouling
B) Oil fouling
C) Lead fouling
D) Gap erosion
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because carbon fouling from fuel comes with a mixture fault, and the idle mixture is correct. C is wrong because lead fouling comes from leaded fuel deposits. D is wrong because gap erosion is wear, not a wet deposit.
notes.explanation: Oil drawn past rings and guides wets the plug; higher rpm airflow clears it, giving white fumes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Oil Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-34
notes.evidence: Then, when intermittent firing starts, combustion assists in emitting the remaining oil. In a few seconds, the engine is running clean with white fumes of evaporating and burning oil coming from the exhaust.

notes.front: After long cruises on lean mixtures with leaded fuel, a plug has hard, solid deposits and the engine misfires. Which fouling is this?
notes.back: D: Lead fouling.
notes.choices:
A) Carbon fouling
B) Graphite fouling
C) Oil fouling
D) Lead fouling
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because carbon fouling is soot from a rich or misfiring mixture. B is wrong because graphite fouling comes from antiseize compound. C is wrong because oil fouling leaves the plug wet with oil.
notes.explanation: Leaded fuel forms lead oxide deposits, and lean cruise is perhaps the setting most likely to cause them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Lead Fouling of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-34
notes.evidence: Lead deposits on combustion chamber surfaces are good electrical conductors at high temperatures and cause misfiring. At low temperatures, the same deposits may be good insulators. In either case, lead formations on aircraft spark plugs prevent their normal operation.

notes.front: A set of plugs at the end of a long service interval shows gaps much wider than specified, and the engine has become hard to start. Which condition is this?
notes.back: A: Gap erosion.
notes.choices:
A) Gap erosion
B) Oil fouling
C) Graphite fouling
D) Lead fouling
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are wrong because fouling is a deposit that stops the spark bridging the gap, while here the gap itself has grown.
notes.explanation: Every spark carries off some electrode metal, and wide gaps raise the magneto’s coming-in speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gap Erosion of Spark Plugs”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: Wide gap settings also raise the coming in speed of a magneto and therefore cause hard starting.

notes.front: A new spark plug slips from your hand and bounces on the concrete floor. It looks undamaged. What do you do?
notes.back: B: Discard it: impact usually causes small, invisible cracks in the insulator.
notes.choices:
A) Install it if it passes a visual check
B) Discard it
C) Install it on a bottom location only
D) Recondition it and then install it
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the cracks are invisible. C is wrong because a cracked insulator is unsafe in any location. D is wrong because the handbook says a dropped plug should be discarded.
notes.explanation: Because the cracks cannot be seen, looking undamaged proves nothing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Removal”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: If a plug is dropped on the floor or other hard surface, it should not be installed in an engine, since the shock of impact usually causes small, invisible cracks in the insulators. A dropped spark plug should be discarded.

notes.front: Why should removed spark plugs go into a drilled spark plug tray?
notes.back: It stops them bumping and damaging insulators and threads, and records where each came from and its rotation.
notes.explanation: Spark plugs are easily damaged, so each should be handled individually.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Removal”, p. 4-35
notes.evidence: This is a drilled tray, which prevents the plugs from bumping against one another and damaging the fragile insulators and threads. Additionally, the tray helps identify where the spark plug came from and its proper rotation.

notes.front: How should an ignition lead be pulled off a spark plug?
notes.back: Straight out, in line with the centreline of the plug barrel.
notes.explanation: A side load can damage the barrel insulator and the ceramic lead terminal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Removal”, p. 4-36
notes.evidence: straight out and in line with the centerline of the plug barrel. If a side load is applied, damage to the barrel insulator and the ceramic lead terminal may result.

notes.front: At every inspection a mechanic cleans each spark plug and refits it in exactly the hole it came from. What is being missed?
notes.back: D: Rotating plugs to new locations, which reverses polarity and equalises electrode wear.
notes.choices:
A) Swapping the ignition leads between magnetos
B) Nothing: plugs must always return to their original hole
C) Changing to a colder heat range each time
D) Rotating plugs to equalise electrode wear
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the handbook recommends rotating plugs to new locations. C is wrong because nothing in the case calls for a different heat range. A is wrong because the leads stay in firing order.
notes.explanation: Plugs that always return to the same hole keep the same polarity, so wear stays uneven.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Ignition Harness”, p. 4-8
notes.evidence: Reversing the polarity during servicing by rotating the plugs to new locations, the plug wear is equalized across the electrodes.

notes.front: Why must spark plug gaps be checked with a round wire-thickness gauge, not a flat one?
notes.back: Massive ground electrodes are shaped round the centre electrode, so a flat gauge gives a wrong reading.
notes.explanation: A plug whose gap is outside the specified range must not be installed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Inspection Prior to Installation”, p. 4-38
notes.evidence: The gap setting should be checked with a round wirethickness gauge. [Figure 4-63] A flat-type gauge gives an incorrect clearance indication because the massive ground electrodes are contoured to the shape of the round center electrode.

notes.front: Before installing a spark plug, where is the antiseize compound applied?
notes.back: A graphite-base compound on the first two or three threads from the electrode end, kept off the electrodes and nose.
notes.explanation: Graphite conducts electricity well, so any on the electrodes could foul the plug permanently.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Installation”, p. 4-38
notes.evidence: coat the first two or three threads from the electrode end of the shell with a graphite base antiseize compound. Prior to application, stir the antiseize compound to ensure thorough mixing. When applying the antiseize compound to the threads, be extremely careful that none of the compound gets on the ground, center electrodes, or on the nose of the plug

notes.front: What does excessive installation torque do to a spark plug?
notes.back: It stretches the shell, opening the seal between shell and insulator: gas tightness is lost or the insulator is damaged.
notes.explanation: The torque keeps screwing the lower shell in after the gasket shoulder has stopped the upper end.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Installation”, p. 4-38
notes.evidence: Shell stretching occurs as excessive torque continues to screw the lower end of the shell into the cylinder after the upper end has been stopped by the gasket shoulder. As the shell stretches, the seal between the shell and core insulator is opened, creating a loss of gas tightness or damage to the core insulator.

notes.front: A spark plug needs a wrench from its very first turn to go into the cylinder. What does this indicate?
notes.back: D: Dirty or damaged threads on the plug or the plug bushing.
notes.choices:
A) Normal: plugs are always installed with a wrench
B) The plug has the wrong heat range
C) The gasket is missing
D) Dirty or damaged threads on the plug or bushing
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because plugs are started by hand without a wrench. B is wrong because heat range does not affect the threads. C is wrong because a missing gasket would not make the threads tight.
notes.explanation: A plug with clean threads screws in with comparative ease by hand until it seats on the gasket.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Installation”, p. 4-38
notes.evidence: In this case, only a small amount of additional tightening torque is needed to compress the gasket to form a gastight seal. If a high torque is needed to install the plug, dirty or damaged threads on either the plug or plug bushing are indicated.

notes.front: When degreasing a spark plug for reconditioning, what must you avoid?
notes.back: Getting solvent in the shielding barrel, and soaking the plug.
notes.explanation: Degreasing with petroleum solvent comes only after the plug has passed its visual check.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Reconditioning Service”, p. 4-36
notes.evidence: If the spark plug passes the visual check, then it should be degreased using petroleum solvent. Take care to keep solvent out of the shielding barrel. Never soak the plugs in solvent.

notes.front: After tightening a spark plug lead’s coupling nut, what should you not do?
notes.back: Check its tightness by twisting the body of the elbow.
notes.explanation: Most manufacturers specify a tool designed to help prevent overtorquing the nut.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Spark Plug Lead Installation”, p. 4-39
notes.evidence: Most manufacturers’ instructions specify the use of a tool designed to help prevent an overtorque condition. After the coupling nut is tightened, avoid checking for tightness by twisting the body of the elbow.

notes.front: How far may breaker contacts be spread for cleaning or inspection?
notes.back: Never more than 1⁄16 inch, with the force applied at the outer end of the mainspring.
notes.explanation: Spread wider, the mainspring is likely to take a permanent set, and the points then bounce or float.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Breaker Point Inspection”, p. 4-39
notes.evidence: always apply the opening force at the outer end of the mainspring and never spread the contacts more than 1⁄16 inch. If the contacts are spread wider than recommended, the mainspring, the spring carrying the movable contact point, is likely to take a permanent set.

notes.front: What does a normal breaker contact surface look like?
notes.back: Dull grey and sandblasted, almost rough, over the area where contact is made.
notes.explanation: That look shows the points have worn in and mated, giving the best electrical contact.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Breaker Point Inspection”, p. 4-39
notes.evidence: The normal contact surface has a dull gray, sandblasted, almost rough appearance over the area where electrical contact is made. [Figure 4-66] This gray, sandblasted appearance indicates that the points have worn in and have mated to each other and are providing the best possible electrical contact.

notes.front: What can cause built-up breaker points?
notes.back: Excessive spring tension giving a slow break, a poor primary condenser, or a loose primary coil connection.
notes.explanation: Metal is carried from one point to the other by the arc as they separate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Breaker Point Inspection”, p. 4-40
notes.evidence: This condition may result from excessive breaker point spring tension that retards the opening of the points or causes a slow, lazy break. It can also be caused by a poor primary condenser or a loose connection at the primary coil. If excessive buildup has occurred, a new breaker assembly must be installed.

notes.front: Magneto breaker points look smoked and smudged, with no pits, peaks or build-up. The engine has been smoking. What is the likely cause, and the remedy?
notes.back: C: Oil vapour or excess cam lubrication; fit a new breaker assembly.
notes.choices:
A) An open condenser; replace the condenser only
B) Normal wear; no action needed
C) Oil vapour or excess cam oil; fit a new breaker assembly
D) Dirt; dress the points with a file
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because an open condenser causes coarse, crystalline frosting. B is wrong because normal points are dull grey, not smudged. D is wrong because dirt causes pitting, and oily points call for a new breaker assembly.
notes.explanation: Conductive oil vapours entering through the ventilator cause arcing and a sooty deposit on the points.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Breaker Point Inspection”, p. 4-40
notes.evidence: Figure 4-69F illustrates oily points that can be recognized by their smoked and smudged appearance and by the lack of any of the previously mentioned irregularities. This condition may be the result of excessive cam lubrication or of oil vapors that may come from within or outside the magneto.

notes.front: According to AC 43.13-1B, should magneto contact point assemblies be dressed or stoned?
notes.back: Generally no, unless the manufacturer’s manuals give procedures and limits.
notes.explanation: Without the manufacturer's procedures and limits there is no approved way to do it, so the circular leaves the points alone.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, para. 8-19 “Magneto Inspection”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: Generally, no attempt should be made to dress or stone contact point assemblies; however, if provided, procedures and limits contained in the manufacturer’s manuals may be followed.

notes.front: Why are coil cases, distributor blocks and rotors wax-coated?
notes.back: The wax helps them resist moisture absorption, carbon tracking and acid deposits.
notes.explanation: They are waxed when new and again at overhaul; dirt or oil strips some of that protection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Dielectric Inspection”, p. 4-41
notes.evidence: Coil cases, distributor blocks, distributor rotors, and other dielectric parts of the ignition system are treated with a wax coating when they are new and again at overhaul. The waxing of dielectrics aids their resistance to moisture absorption, carbon tracking, and acid deposits.

notes.front: Why must a turbine ignition system give a spark of high heat intensity?
notes.back: Turbine engines often run in the low temperatures of high altitude, so a high voltage arcs across a wide igniter gap.
notes.explanation: Fuel ignites readily in ideal conditions, but reliability is needed across widely varying ones.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-43
notes.evidence: The fuel in turbine engines can be ignited readily in ideal atmospheric conditions, but since they often operate in the low temperatures of high altitudes, it is imperative that the system be capable of supplying a high heat intensity spark. Thus, a high-voltage is supplied to arc across a wide igniter spark gap,

notes.front: In an older capacitor-type turbine ignition system, the storage capacitor charges up to a maximum of approximately {{c1::4}} joules.
notes.explanation: Repeated pulses through the rectifier build the charge before the contactor closes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-43
notes.evidence: This voltage causes a pulse of current to flow into the storage capacitor through the rectifier, which limits the flow to a single direction. With repeated pulses, the storage capacitor assumes a charge, up to a maximum of approximately 4 joules.

notes.front: A turbine-powered aircraft is lining up for takeoff. Which ignition mode is used to guard against a flameout?
notes.back: B: Continuous ignition.
notes.choices:
A) No ignition: the flame is self-sustaining
B) Continuous ignition
C) Start ignition at full energy throughout the flight
D) Shower of sparks
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because takeoff is listed as a mode that uses continuous ignition. C is wrong because continuous ignition runs at a lower voltage and energy level than starting. D is wrong because the shower of sparks is a piston engine starting aid.
notes.explanation: Takeoff is one of the critical flight modes in which continuous ignition is used to relight the fuel after a flameout.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Turbine Engine Ignition Systems”, p. 4-43
notes.evidence: Examples of critical flight modes that use continuous ignition are takeoff, landing, and some abnormal and emergency situations.

notes.front: An exciter’s fan cooling-air duct is found disconnected on an aircraft whose crew often use continuous ignition for long periods. What is the risk?
notes.back: D: The exciter can overheat during long use of continuous ignition.
notes.choices:
A) None, because exciters work only during starting
B) The igniter gap will close up
C) The engine will lose its permanent magnet generator
D) The exciter may overheat
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because continuous ignition keeps the exciter working in flight. B is wrong because loss of cooling air is not linked to the igniter gap. C is wrong because the duct cools the exciter, not the generator.
notes.explanation: The exciters are air-cooled precisely to prevent overheating during extended continuous ignition.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Capacitor Discharge Exciter Unit”, p. 4-45
notes.evidence: This is why the exciters are air cooled to prevent overheating during long use of continuous ignition.

notes.front: Why is an igniter plug’s gap much larger than a spark plug’s?
notes.back: Operating pressures are much lower, so the spark can arc more easily.
notes.explanation: The heat of the intense spark also keeps electrode fouling to a minimum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Igniter Plugs”, p. 4-45
notes.evidence: The electrode gap of the typical igniter plug is designed much larger than that of a spark plug since the operating pressures are much lower and the spark can arc more easily than in a spark plug. Finally, electrode fouling, common to the spark plug, is minimized by the heat of the high-intensity spark.

notes.front: Which igniter plug runs much cooler because it does not project into the combustion chamber liner?
notes.back: C: The constrained-gap igniter plug.
notes.choices:
A) The annular-gap igniter plug
B) A long reach igniter
C) The constrained-gap igniter plug
D) A massive-electrode spark plug
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are the same plug: the annular-gap, or long reach, igniter projects into the liner. D is wrong because spark plugs belong to reciprocating engines.
notes.explanation: Its spark arcs beyond the face of the liner rather than staying close to the plug.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Igniter Plugs”, p. 4-45
notes.evidence: It operates at a much cooler temperature because it does not project into the combustion-chamber liner. This is possible because the spark does not remain close to the plug, but arcs beyond the face of the combustion chamber liner.

notes.front: How can a turbine igniter be checked during a start?
notes.back: By listening for a snapping noise as the starter begins to turn the engine.
notes.explanation: Removing the igniter to watch it spark is not common practice and is used only if the maintenance manual allows it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Check System Operation”, p. 4-46
notes.evidence: The igniter can be checked by listening for a snapping noise as the engine begins to turn, driven by the starter. Though the following procedure is not common practice and should only be used when the maintenance manual suggests it as an alternative method

notes.front: On which igniter plugs must deposits on the firing end not be removed?
notes.back: Low-voltage igniters. High-voltage igniters may have the firing end cleaned to help inspection.
notes.explanation: Before inspecting either type, residue is wiped only from the shell exterior with a dry cloth.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Removal, Maintenance, & Installation of Ignition System Components”, p. 4-47
notes.evidence: Before inspection, remove residue from the shell exterior using a dry cloth. Do not remove any deposits or residue from the firing end of the low-voltage igniters. High-voltage igniters can have the firing end cleaned to aid in inspection.

notes.front: Why must an activated turbine ignition system be treated with great caution?
notes.back: Its high energy and voltage can cause injury or death to anyone who touches it.
notes.explanation: Its capacitors store a high-energy charge that is released at high voltage across the wide igniter gap.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Check System Operation”, p. 4-46
notes.evidence: Caution: The high energy level and voltage associated with turbine ignition systems can cause injury or death to personnel coming into contact with the activated system.

notes.front: Right after a failed start attempt, a mechanic reaches to unplug the high-voltage cable from an igniter. What should happen first?
notes.back: C: Disconnect the exciter’s low-voltage input, then wait at least one minute for stored energy to dissipate.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the system is safe once the start switch is off
B) Wear gloves and go ahead
C) Disconnect the exciter input and wait at least one minute
D) Wait ten seconds
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the capacitors can still hold energy. B is wrong because the handbook requires the energy to dissipate, not just protection. D is wrong because the stated wait is at least one minute.
notes.explanation: The system stores energy that can cause injury or death, so it must be allowed to dissipate first.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Removal, Maintenance, & Installation of Ignition System Components”, p. 4-47
notes.evidence: from the ignition exciter unit and wait at least one minute to permit the stored energy to dissipate before disconnecting the high-voltage cable from the igniter.

notes.front: What turns almost all reciprocating engines for starting?
notes.back: A form of electric motor geared to the engine.
notes.explanation: Modern turbines instead use electric motors, starter-generators and air turbine starters.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Starting Systems: Introduction”, p. 5-1
notes.evidence: There are only a few types or methods used to turn the engine. Almost all reciprocating engines use a form of electric motor geared to the engine. Modern turbine engines use electric motors, starter/generators (electric motor and a generator in the same housing), and air turbine starters.

notes.front: A trainee says a turbine starter can drop out the moment the engine lights off, just as a piston engine’s does. Is that right?
notes.back: D: No. It must keep assisting until the engine reaches a self-sustaining speed.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, both starters drop out at first firing
B) Yes, but only for starter-generators
C) No, it must stay engaged for the whole flight
D) No, it must assist until self-sustaining speed
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because only the reciprocating starter stops once the engine fires. B is wrong because the rule applies to every turbine starter type. C is wrong because the starter is cut off once self-sustaining speed is passed.
notes.explanation: At light-off a turbine cannot yet accelerate on its own, unlike a piston engine that has fired.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Engine Starting Systems: Introduction”, p. 5-1
notes.evidence: Then, the starter must continue to help the engine accelerate to a self-sustaining speed. Turbine engine starters have a critical role in starting of the engine. If the starter turns the turbine engine up to a self-sustaining speed, the engine start process will be successful.

notes.front: What kind of motor is the typical starter motor?
notes.back: A 12- or 24-volt series-wound motor that develops high starting torque.
notes.explanation: Its torque passes through reduction gears to the overload release clutch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starter”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: The typical starter motor is a 12- or 24-volt, series-wound motor that develops high starting torque. The torque of the motor is transmitted through reduction gears to the overload release clutch.

notes.front: A light aircraft’s engine is cranked by an electric motor whose drive gear moves out to engage a ring gear on the propeller hub. What kind of starter is this?
notes.back: A: A direct cranking electric starter.
notes.choices:
A) A direct cranking electric starter
B) An inertia starter
C) An air turbine starter
D) A starter-generator
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because an inertia starter cranks with a flywheel’s stored energy. C is wrong because an air turbine starter is air-driven and used on turbines. D is wrong because a starter-generator stays permanently engaged and is used on turbines.
notes.explanation: Most small reciprocating aircraft use direct cranking electric starting, and this is one of its layouts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starting System for Small Aircraft”, p. 5-6
notes.evidence: Other engines use a starter that drives a ring gear mounted to the propeller hub. [Figure 5-10] It uses an electric motor and a drive gear that engages as the motor is energized and spins the gear, which moves out and engages the ring gear on the propeller hub cranking the engine for start.

notes.front: You crank an engine for 1 minute, let the starter cool for 1 minute, then crank for another minute without a start. How long must the starter now cool?
notes.back: B: 5 minutes.
notes.choices:
A) 30 seconds
B) 5 minutes
C) 2 minutes
D) 1 minute
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because even the first crank needs at least 1 minute of cooling. D is wrong because 1 minute applies only after the first crank. C is wrong because the handbook gives 5 minutes after a second crank.
notes.explanation: After a second or later 1-minute cranking period the cooling time rises from 1 minute to 5.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starting System for Large Reciprocating Engines”, p. 5-6
notes.evidence: After energizing the starter for 1 minute, it should be allowed to cool for at least 1 minute. After a second or subsequent cranking period of 1 minute, it should cool for 5 minutes.

notes.front: In a manually engaged small-aircraft starter, what protects the drive pinion once the engine starts?
notes.back: The overrunning action of the clutch, until the shift lever is released.
notes.explanation: The engine then turns faster than the starter, and the clutch lets it overrun the pinion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Direct Cranking Electric Starting System for Small Aircraft”, p. 5-6
notes.evidence: When the engine starts, the overrunning action of the clutch protects the starter drive pinion until the shift lever can be released to disengage the pinion.

notes.front: As a rule, when should starter brushes be replaced?
notes.back: When worn down to about one-half of their original length.
notes.explanation: Brush spring tension must also be enough to hold the brushes firmly on the commutator.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Starting System Maintenance Practices”, p. 5-7
notes.evidence: As a rule, starter brushes should be replaced when worn down to approximately one-half the original length. Brush spring tension should be sufficient to give brushes a good firm contact with the commutator.

notes.front: Why should emery paper or carborundum never be used to clean a starter commutator?
notes.back: They can cause shorting; use double-0 sandpaper or a brush seating stone.
notes.explanation: Moving the paper or stone back and forth also avoids wearing a groove.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Reciprocating Engine Starting System Maintenance Practices”, p. 5-7
notes.evidence: The sandpaper or stone should be moved back and forth across the commutator to avoid wearing a groove. Emery paper or carborundum should never be used for this purpose because of their possible shorting action.

notes.front: A light aircraft’s starter motor spins, but the crankshaft does not turn. Which of these is a listed probable cause?
notes.back: D: The starter lever is adjusted to work the switch without engaging the pinion.
notes.choices:
A) A low battery
B) A defective master switch
C) A dirty, worn commutator
D) Starter lever adjusted to work the switch without engaging the pinion
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong because the table lists them under a starter that drags. B is wrong because a defective master switch stops the starter operating at all.
notes.explanation: If the switch closes before the pinion meshes, the motor runs free; the lever must move the pinion first.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Troubleshooting Small Aircraft Starting Systems”, p. 5-8
notes.evidence: Starter lever adjusted to activate switch without engaging pinion with

notes.front: In a turbine start sequence, when is the ignition turned on?
notes.back: As soon as the starter has accelerated the compressor enough to establish airflow; the fuel follows.
notes.explanation: There must be enough airflow to support combustion before the air-fuel mixture is ignited.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gas Turbine Engine Starters”, p. 5-8
notes.evidence: As soon as the starter has accelerated the compressor sufficiently to establish airflow through the engine, the ignition is turned on followed by the fuel. The exact sequence of the starting procedure is important since there must be sufficient airflow through the engine to support combustion before the air-fuel mixture is ignited.

notes.front: During a turbine start the starter drops out just after light-off; rpm stops rising while exhaust gas temperature climbs. What went wrong?
notes.back: A: The starter stopped assisting too early, well short of the speed needed, delaying the start into a hot or hung start.
notes.choices:
A) The starter cut out too early
B) Ignition came on before airflow was established
C) The fuel came on after the ignition
D) Nothing: rising temperature is normal on every start
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the engine did light off; the trouble began only when the starter dropped out. C is wrong because ignition before fuel is the correct order. D is wrong because a stalled rpm with climbing temperature is a hung or hot start.
notes.explanation: The starter must help considerably above self-accelerating speed to avoid exactly this.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Gas Turbine Engine Starters”, p. 5-8
notes.evidence: The starter must continue to assist the engine considerably above the self-accelerating speed to avoid a delay in the starting cycle, which would result in a hot or hung false start or a combination of both.

notes.front: Why are starter-generators desirable on turbine aircraft?
notes.back: One unit does both jobs, so weight falls and fewer spare parts are needed.
notes.explanation: It saves weight and space by switching from starter to generator once the engine is self-sustaining.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Electric Starting Systems & Starter Generator Starting System”, p. 5-10
notes.evidence: Starter generator units are desirable from an economic standpoint, since one unit performs the functions of both starter and generator. Additionally, the total weight of starting system components is reduced and fewer spare parts are required.

notes.front: Starter-generator versus direct cranking starter on a turbine: how does each engage the engine?
notes.back: The starter-generator is permanently engaged through drive gears; a direct cranking starter must disengage after the start.
notes.explanation: Because it stays engaged, the starter-generator can switch to generating once the engine runs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Electric Starting Systems & Starter Generator Starting System”, p. 5-10
notes.evidence: The starter generator is permanently engaged with the engine shaft through the necessary drive gears, while the direct cranking starter must employ some means of disengaging the starter from the shaft after the engine has started.

notes.front: Why does the battery cutout relay disconnect the battery during a starter-generator start?
notes.back: The starter motor’s heavy drain would damage the battery.
notes.explanation: It is one of three relays that close when the battery and start switch is turned on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Electric Starting Systems & Starter Generator Starting System”, p. 5-11
notes.evidence: the battery cutout relay disconnects the battery. Opening the battery circuit is necessary because the heavy drain of the starter motor would damage the battery.

notes.front: During a start, a starter-generator’s current draw falls from its peak to 180 amps as the engine accelerates. What happens next?
notes.back: B: The undercurrent relay opens and the start operation ends.
notes.choices:
A) The battery cutout relay closes to add battery power
B) The undercurrent relay opens and the start ends
C) The starter keeps running until the pilot presses stop
D) The motor relay closes for a second start
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the cutout relay is de-energised, not re-closed. C is wrong because the stop switch is only for an engine that fails to reach that speed. D is wrong because the motor relay is de-energised.
notes.explanation: Current below 200 amps opens the undercurrent relay, which de-energises the start relays.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Electric Starting Systems & Starter Generator Starting System”, p. 5-11
notes.evidence: As it decreases to less than 200 amps, the undercurrent relay opens. This action breaks the circuit from the positive bus to the coils of the motor, ignition, and battery cutout relays. The de-energizing of these relay coils halts the start operation.

notes.front: On a starter-generator start attempt you hear the starter turning, but the engine does not rotate. What does the troubleshooting guide conclude?
notes.back: A: The starter drive shaft in the component drive gearbox is sheared.
notes.choices:
A) A sheared starter drive shaft
B) Low supply voltage
C) A defective power switch
D) A defective ignition system
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong because they would stop the starter turning at all. D is wrong because ignition faults stop light-off, not engine rotation.
notes.explanation: A starter that rotates without turning the engine has lost its mechanical link to it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Troubleshooting a Starter Generator Starting System”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: Listen for sounds of starter rotation during an attempted start. If the starter rotates but the engine does not, the drive shaft is sheared.

notes.front: How does an air turbine starter compare with an electric starter for the same engine?
notes.back: It weighs one-fourth to one-half as much and develops considerably more torque.
notes.explanation: It is designed to give high starting torque from a small, lightweight source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starters”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: Air turbine starters are designed to provide high starting torque from a small, lightweight source. The typical air turbine starter weighs from one-fourth to one-half as much as an electric starter capable of starting the same engine. It is capable of developing considerable more torque than the electric starter.

notes.front: What does the sprag clutch in an air turbine starter do?
notes.back: It engages as the rotor starts turning and disengages when the drive coupling outruns the rotor, letting the gear train coast to a halt.
notes.explanation: The output shaft and coupling keep turning with the engine after that.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starters”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: The sprag clutch assembly engages automatically as soon as the rotor starts to turn but disengages as soon as the drive coupling turns more rapidly than the rotor side. When the starter reaches this overrun speed, the action of the sprag clutch allows the gear train to coast to a halt.

notes.front: Before an air turbine start, the duct pressure reads 22 psi from the only air source available. What should you do?
notes.back: A: Do not attempt the start until a supply giving at least about 30 psi is available.
notes.choices:
A) Wait for a supply of at least about 30 psi
B) Connect a second air source at the same time
C) Start anyway: any pressure turns the turbine
D) Start and hold the starter engaged longer
notes.choicesExplained: C is wrong because the pressure must be high enough for a complete start. B is wrong because only one source is used at a time. D is wrong because low pressure risks an incomplete start, which is not fixed by holding the starter longer.
notes.explanation: The ducts need pressure high enough for a complete start, with a normal minimum of about 30 psi.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starters”, p. 5-12
notes.evidence: The pressure in the ducts must be high enough to provide for a complete start with a normal limit minimum of about 30 psi. When starting engines with an air turbine starter, always check the duct pressure prior to the start attempt.

notes.front: What does normal maintenance of an air turbine starter include?
notes.back: Checking the oil level, inspecting the magnetic chip detector for metal particles, and checking for leaks.
notes.explanation: The starter has its own oil in the transmission housing, separate from the engine’s oil system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starters”, p. 5-13
notes.evidence: Normal maintenance for air turbine starters includes checking the oil level, inspecting the magnetic chip detector for metal particles, and checking for leaks.

notes.front: Small fuzzy particles are found on an air turbine starter’s magnetic drain plug. What do they indicate?
notes.back: Normal wear; no remedial action is required.
notes.explanation: Coarser particles, such as chips or slivers, would instead point to internal trouble.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), “Air Turbine Starter Troubleshooting Guide”, p. 5-16
notes.evidence: Small fuzzy particles indicate normal wear. • No remedial action required.
